claim: Amphid neurons in C. elegans form a multicellular rosette at the comma stage of embryogenesis.
source: Using phalloidin staining, we observed a multicellular rosette at the comma stage of C. elegans embryogenesis (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The cnd-1/NeuroD promoter drives PH::GFP expression in 9 of the 12 amphid neurons (ADF, ASE, ASG, ASH, ASI, ASJ, AWA, AWB, AWC).
source: Specifically, the cnd-1p::PH::GFP marker labels 9 of the 12 amphid neurons (ADF, ASE, ASG, ASH, ASI, ASJ, AWA, AWB, AWC).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observation using the cnd-1p::PH::GFP marker and cell lineage tracing.

claim: Five non-amphid neurons (AIB, AVB, AUA, RIV, URB) transiently engage in the amphid rosette and disengage about 40 minutes later.
source: Surprisingly, the marker showed that five other neurons (AIB, AVB, AUA, RIV, URB) are also engaged in the rosette. However, judging by cell shape changes, these non-amphid neurons disengage from the rosette about 40 min later.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging data showing cell shape changes over time.

claim: PAR-6 is localized to the center of the amphid rosette.
source: We found that PAR-6 is localized to the center of the rosette (Figure 1C), suggesting that the rosette is a polarized structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DYF-7 is localized to the rosette center.
source: Furthermore, DYF-7, which is required for anchoring the dendrite tips during retrograde extension (Heiman and Shaham, 2009), is also localized to the rosette center (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D and references prior work on DYF-7 function.

claim: DYF-7 is required for anchoring the dendrite tips during retrograde extension.
source: Furthermore, DYF-7, which is required for anchoring the dendrite tips during retrograde extension (Heiman and Shaham, 2009), is also localized to the rosette center (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Heiman and Shaham, 2009.

claim: Amphid dendrites extend in two distinct steps: first anterior-directed growth, then posterior-directed growth.
source: These results show that the dendrites extend in two distinct steps: first, anterior-directed growth that extrudes the nascent dendrites from the neuronal cell bodies and brings the dendrite endings to the sensory depression at the nose, followed by posterior-directed growth that is concomitant with movement of the neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: During anterior-directed dendrite extension, the cell bodies remain largely stationary.
source: During this period, the cell bodies remain largely stationary (dashed lines in Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The rosette vertex is aligned with the leading edge of the migrating epidermis, specifically the hyp5 cell.
source: We found that prior to anterior movement of the dendrite tips, the rosette vertex is aligned with the leading edge of the migrating epidermis, specifically the hyp5 cell.
evidence: The claim is based on 3D time-lapse imaging data using mCherry::PAR-6 and DLG-1::GFP reporters.

claim: The dendrite tips are situated in an indentation at the leading edge of hyp5 as the epidermis migrates anteriorly.
source: As the epidermis migrates anteriorly, an indentation can be observed at the leading edge of hyp5. The dendrite tips are situated in the indentation (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The anterior movement of the dendrite tips is correlated with the anterior migration of the leading edge of hyp5.
source: Furthermore, the anterior movement of the dendrite tips is correlated with the anterior migration of the leading edge of hyp5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ELT-1 is a GATA transcription factor necessary to specify epidermal fate.
source: ELT-1 is a GATA transcription factor that is necessary to specify epidermal fate (Page et al., 1997) and that activates the expression of its target, lin-26 (Landmann et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Page et al., 1997 and Landmann et al., 2004.

claim: ELT-1 activates the expression of its target, lin-26.
source: ELT-1 is a GATA transcription factor that is necessary to specify epidermal fate (Page et al., 1997) and that activates the expression of its target, lin-26 (Landmann et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Landmann et al., 2004.

claim: In elt-1(RNAi) embryos with high lin-26::GFP expression, the epidermis and amphid dendrites develop normally.
source: 24 out of 79 elt-1(RNAi) embryos showed high level of expression of lin-26::GFP, suggesting the RNAi was not effective in these cases. These embryos exhibited more or less normal anterior migration of the epidermis and the amphid dendrites also developed normally, showing movement that was correlated with the epidermal cells and that brought the dendrite endings to the sensory depression (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experimental data with lin-26::GFP marker expression.

claim: In elt-1(RNAi) embryos with low lin-26::GFP expression, the epidermis undergoes partial anterior migration and dendrites show partial anterior extension.
source: In contrast, in 29 out of 79 embryos, low levels of lin-26::GFP expression were observed, suggesting a moderate effect of RNAi. In these embryos, the epidermis underwent partial anterior migration but stopped before covering the head completely, and the dendrites also showed partial anterior extension, stopping at the position where the epidermis stopped (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experimental data with lin-26::GFP marker expression.

claim: Dendrite tips remain coupled to the leading edge of the epidermis even as the epidermis retracts posteriorly in some elt-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: Intriguingly, the dendrite tips remained coupled to the leading edge of the epidermis even as the epidermis retracted posteriorly after failing to enclose the head in some embryos (dashed lines in Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging data of elt-1(RNAi) embryos shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In elt-1(RNAi) embryos with minimal or no lin-26::GFP expression, dendrite extension is abolished even though the rosette forms normally.
source: Finally, in the embryos with the strongest RNAi effect (26/79), where minimal or no lin-26::GFP expression remained, dendrite extension was abolished, even though the rosette formed normally (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experimental data with lin-26::GFP marker expression.

claim: Dendrite extension requires the anterior migration of the epidermis.
source: These results suggest that the dendrite tips are attached to the leading edge of the epidermis and that dendrite extension requires the anterior migration of the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the elt-1(RNAi) experimental results showing correlation between epidermal migration and dendrite extension.

claim: DYF-7 is expressed by amphid neurons and not in epidermis.
source: As previously described, we found that DYF-7 was expressed by amphid neurons and not in epidermis.
evidence: The claim is based on expression pattern analysis using a dyf-7 promoter-driven construct.

claim: DYF-7 localizes to the dendrite tips.
source: As expected from its localization to the rosette vertex (Figure 1B), it localized to the dendrite tips (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HMR-1 is localized at the dendrite tips in addition to epidermal cell junctions.
source: HMR-1 was observed at the dendrite tips in addition to its known localization at epidermal cell junctions (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SAX-7 is localized to the epidermal cell junctions and along the amphid dendrites.
source: We found that SAX-7 is localized to the epidermal cell junctions and along the amphid dendrites (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data using a fosmid-based GFP reporter shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SAX-7 functions redundantly with HMR-1 in blastomere compaction during C. elegans gastrulation.
source: SAX-7 has been shown to function redundantly with HMR-1 in blastomere compaction during C. elegans gastrulation (Grana et al., 2010), and to mediate the interaction between the epidermis and the dendrite of the PVD neuron (Dong et al., 2013; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Grana et al., 2010.

claim: SAX-7 mediates the interaction between the epidermis and the dendrite of the PVD neuron.
source: SAX-7 has been shown to function redundantly with HMR-1 in blastomere compaction during C. elegans gastrulation (Grana et al., 2010), and to mediate the interaction between the epidermis and the dendrite of the PVD neuron (Dong et al., 2013; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Dong et al., 2013 and Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: CRISPR-tagged DLG-1 shows localization on both the apical junctions of epidermal cells and the amphid dendrite tips.
source: Furthermore, while a DLG-1/Dlg1 reporter used initially in this study (xnIs17) showed expression only in the epidermis (Figure 2A), we found that a more recently-developed CRISPR tagged DLG-1 (Heppert et al., 2018) showed localization on both the apical junctions of epidermal cells and the amphid dendrite tips (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data using CRISPR-tagged DLG-1 shown in Figure 3D and comparison with a different reporter.

claim: In the majority of dyf-7(m537) mutant embryos (84/88), the dendrite tip reached the sensory depression but detached afterwards when the cell bodies moved posteriorly.
source: In the majority of the dyf-7(m537) mutant embryos (84/88), the dendrite tip reached the sensory depression, but detached afterwards when the cell bodies moved posteriorly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the known function of dyf-7 in the later steps of dendrite extension.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dyf-7(m537) mutant embryos.

claim: In a small fraction of dyf-7(m537) embryos (4/88), dendrites of one amphid extended partially and the tip failed to reach the sensory depression.
source: However, in a small fraction of dyf-7(m537) embryos (4/88), dendrites of one of the amphids extended partially and the tip failed to reach the sensory depression (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dyf-7(m537) mutant embryos shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DYF-7 plays a role in the attachment between epidermal cells and dendrite tips during the initial anterior extension of dendrites.
source: This result suggests that DYF-7 also plays a role in the attachment between epidermal cells and dendrite tips during the initial anterior extension of dendrites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that some dyf-7(m537) embryos show defects in anterior dendrite extension.

claim: In 34/102 of dex-1(ns42) embryos, the amphid dendrite tips detached during the later posterior-directed dendrite extension.
source: In 34/102 of the dex-1(ns42) embryos, the amphid dendrite tips detached during the later posterior-directed dendrite extension.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dex-1(ns42) mutant embryos.

claim: 1/102 dex-1(ns42) embryos showed defects in the early anterior-directed extension.
source: 1/102 dex-1(ns42) embryos showed defects in the early anterior-directed extension, suggesting that DEX-1 also functions during attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dex-1(ns42) mutant embryos shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No dendrite extension defects were found in sax-7(ky146), hmr-1(RNAi) or sax-7(ky146);hmr-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: We did not find dendrite extension defects in sax-7(ky146), hmr-1(RNAi) or sax-7(ky146);hmr-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of single and double mutant/RNAi embryos shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Neither sax-7(ky146) nor hmr-1(RNAi) enhanced the phenotype of dyf-7(m537) in the anterior extension of the dendrites.
source: Neither sax-7(ky146) nor hmr-1(RNAi) enhanced the phenotype of dyf-7(m537) in the anterior extension of the dendrites.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of double mutant/RNAi combinations.

claim: In dyf-7(m537);sax-7(ky146);hmr-1(RNAi) triple loss of function embryos, there is a significant increase in anterior dendrite extension defects compared to dyf-7(m537).
source: However, in dyf-7(m537);sax-7(ky146);hmr-1(RNAi) triple loss of function embryos, we found a significant increase in anterior dendrite extension defects compared to dyf-7(m537) (16/88, Fisher's exact test (two-tailed); threshold of significance was adjusted by Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis with statistical testing shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: DYF-7, SAX-7 and HMR-1 act redundantly in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
source: The significantly higher penetrance suggests that DYF-7, SAX-7 and HMR-1 act redundantly in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing enhanced phenotype in triple mutants.

claim: 6 out of 72 dyf-7; sax-7; dlg-1(RNAi) embryos arrested before reaching the 1.5-fold stage, suggesting that epidermal migration was disrupted.
source: In contrast, 6 out of 72 dyf-7; sax-7; dlg-1(RNAi) embryos arrested before reaching the 1.5-fold stage, suggesting that epidermal migration was disrupted.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of triple mutant/RNAi embryos.

claim: In dyf-7; sax-7; dlg-1(RNAi) embryos that developed to the 1.5-fold stage, 15 out of 66 showed a defect in anterior extension of amphid dendrites on one side.
source: In the remaining 66 embryos that developed to the 1.5-fold stage and beyond, 15 showed a defect in anterior extension of amphid dendrites on one side of the embryo while the dendrite tips of the contralateral side reached the sensory depression (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of triple mutant/RNAi embryos shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The frequency of anterior extension defects in dyf-7; sax-7; dlg-1(RNAi) (23%) is significantly higher than that of dyf-7(m537) (5%).
source: This frequency (15/66, or 23%) is significantly higher than that of dyf-7(m537) (4/88, or 5%), suggesting that DLG-1 also functions in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical comparison of phenotypic frequencies between different genotypes.

claim: DLG-1 functions in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
source: This frequency (15/66, or 23%) is significantly higher than that of dyf-7(m537) (4/88, or 5%), suggesting that DLG-1 also functions in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing enhanced phenotype in triple mutants.

claim: In 20% of par-6(M/Z) embryos (5/25), DYF-7 showed a more diffuse localization around the rosette center.
source: In 20% of the par-6(M/Z) embryos (5/25), DYF-7 showed a more diffuse localization around the rosette center (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The size of the DYF-7::GFP signal at the vertex increased significantly in par-6(M/Z) embryos compared to wild type (1.36 ± 0.25 µm in WT vs 2.27 ± 0.41 µm).
source: The size of the DYF-7::GFP signal at the vertex increased significantly (1.36 ± 0.25 µm in the WT vs 2.27 ± 0.41 µm, student t-test, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative imaging analysis with statistical testing shown in Figure 4C.

claim: During later steps of dendrite extension, DYF-7 signal was spread along the dendrites in par-6(M/Z) embryos (7/25).
source: Furthermore, during later steps of dendrite extension, DYF-7 signal was spread along the dendrites in par-6(M/Z) embryos (7/25) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PAR-6 regulates the localization of DYF-7.
source: Nonetheless, these phenotypes suggest that PAR-6 regulates the localization of DYF-7 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DYF-7 localization is altered in par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: PAR-6 is required for apical junction formation in epidermal cells by regulating the localization of HMR-1 and DLG-1.
source: A previous study showed that PAR-6 is required for apical junction formation in epidermal cells by regulating the localization of HMR-1 and DLG-1 (Totong et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Totong et al., 2007.

claim: 17 of the 25 par-6(M/Z) embryos arrested early (at 1.5-fold or soon after), indicating early malformation of the epidermis.
source: As expected, 17 of the 25 par-6(M/Z) embryos arrested early (at 1.5-fold or soon after), indicating early malformation of the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: Among par-6(M/Z) embryos that arrested early, five showed partial dendrite extension.
source: Among these, five embryos showed partial dendrite extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 8 of the 25 par-6(M/Z) embryos developed to the 2-fold stage, suggesting that epidermal morphogenesis was more or less normal.
source: 8 of the 25 par-6(M/Z) embryos developed to the 2-fold stage, suggesting that in these embryos epidermal morphogenesis was more or less normal beyond the stage where the dendrite tips normally reach the sensory depression.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: Among par-6(M/Z) embryos that developed to the 2-fold stage, one showed little dendrite extension.
source: Among these eight embryos, we found one in which the dendrites showed little extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of par-6(M/Z) embryos shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PAR-6 may play a role in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
source: This result raises the possibility that PAR-6 may play a role in the attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on limited observations in par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: The amphid rosette-mediated mechanism for collective neurite outgrowth is different from the classical pioneer-follower model.
source: Our results revealed a mechanism where a multicellular rosette organizes collective neurite outgrowth, which is different from the classical pioneer-follower model in coordinating a group of neurites to grow in the same direction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations showing rosette-mediated collective extension rather than pioneer-follower dynamics.

claim: Multicellular rosettes have been found in diverse organisms and developmental contexts, including C. elegans ventral nerve cord assembly.
source: Multicellular rosettes have been found in diverse organisms and developmental contexts, including C. elegans in terms of the assembly of the ventral nerve cord (Harding et al., 2014; Paré et al., 2014; Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on rosettes in various contexts.

claim: In previously reported contexts, rosettes are used to orchestrate cell intercalation and collective migration.
source: However, in these previously reported contexts, rosettes are used to orchestrate cell intercalation and collective migration.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from cited prior work on rosette function.

claim: The amphid rosette remains stable, unlike rosettes in other contexts that undergo dynamic formation and resolution.
source: In contrast, the amphid rosette remains stable. It is not clear what causes the difference in cellular behaviors between the amphid rosette and the others.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of the amphid rosette compared to knowledge of other rosettes.

claim: Electron microscopy of the developing amphid suggests the presence of tight junctions between the dendrites.
source: Indeed, electron microscopy of the developing amphid suggests the presence of tight junctions between the dendrites; in the mature structure, tight junctions are present between each of the neurons and the sheath glial cell (Low et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Low et al., 2019.

claim: In the mature amphid structure, tight junctions are present between each of the neurons and the sheath glial cell.
source: Indeed, electron microscopy of the developing amphid suggests the presence of tight junctions between the dendrites; in the mature structure, tight junctions are present between each of the neurons and the sheath glial cell (Low et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Low et al., 2019.

claim: Tight junctions in the amphid define an outward-facing apical surface.
source: These junctions define an outward-facing apical surface (Low et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Low et al., 2019.

claim: The initial extension of the amphid dendrites is driven by the migrating skin through physical attachment.
source: We also showed that the initial extension of the amphid dendrites is driven by the migrating skin through physical attachment.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations showing correlation between epidermal migration and dendrite extension, and elt-1(RNAi) results.

claim: Retrograde extension of amphid dendrites occurs in at least two steps: first, neurons attach to the migrating epidermis which pulls dendrite endings anteriorly; then, neuron cell bodies migrate away, pulling dendrites posteriorly.
source: Thus, retrograde extension of amphid dendrites occurs in at least two steps: first, neurons attach to the migrating epidermis, which pulls the dendrite endings anteriorly to the developing nose; then, the neuron cell bodies migrate away, pulling the dendrites posteriorly as they move.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging observations and experimental manipulations.

claim: Attachment to a moving target has been proposed to underlie axon extension of the M2 pharyngeal neuron in C. elegans.
source: Attachment to a moving target, similar to the first step, has been proposed to underlie axon extension of the M2 pharyngeal neuron in C. elegans (Pilon, 2014) as well as lateral line 'axon towing' in zebrafish (Gilmour et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Pilon, 2014.

claim: Attachment to a moving target has been proposed to underlie lateral line 'axon towing' in zebrafish.
source: Attachment to a moving target, similar to the first step, has been proposed to underlie axon extension of the M2 pharyngeal neuron in C. elegans (Pilon, 2014) as well as lateral line 'axon towing' in zebrafish (Gilmour et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Gilmour et al., 2004.

claim: Movement of neuronal cell bodies away from their attachment sites has been proposed to underlie olfactory axon development in zebrafish.
source: Movement of neuronal cell bodies away from their attachment sites, similar to the second step, has been proposed to underlie olfactory axon development in zebrafish (Breau et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Breau et al., 2017.

claim: The molecular mechanisms for initial attachment of dendrite tips to the epidermis during anterior extension differ from those for anchoring dendrite tips at the sensory depression during neuronal cell body movement.
source: Interestingly, the molecular mechanisms appear to be different in terms of the initial attachment of the dendrite tips/rosette vertex to the epidermis during anterior extension and the anchoring of dendrite tips at the sensory depression during the subsequent movement of neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different phenotypic penetrance of dyf-7 mutations in the two phases and the redundancy with other adhesion molecules.

claim: dyf-7 loss of function causes detachment of the dendrite tips from the sensory depression in 100% of embryos during the later phase.
source: In the latter case, dyf-7 loss of function causes detachment of the dendrite tips from the sensory depression in 100% of the embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dyf-7 mutants.

claim: The same dyf-7 allele only causes dendrite tip detachment from the migrating skin in 5% of embryos during anterior extension.
source: The same allele, however, only causes a mild phenotype during anterior extension where the dendrite tips detached from the migrating skin in 5% of the embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic analysis of dyf-7 mutants.

claim: SAX-7 and HMR-1 function redundantly with DYF-7 to mediate the attachment of the dendrite tips to the skin during anterior extension.
source: Furthermore, in anterior extension, we showed that SAX-7 and HMR-1 function redundantly with DYF-7 to mediate the attachment of the dendrite tips to the skin.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotype in triple mutants.

claim: Transition zone proteins in cilia function in dendrite extension.
source: In comparison, recent work suggests that transition zone proteins in cilia function in dendrite extension (Schouteden et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Schouteden et al., 2015.

claim: Transition zone proteins do not appear to be localized to the amphid dendrite tips until the 2-fold stage, about an hour after skin-driven anterior extension is complete.
source: However, transition zone proteins do not appear to be localized to the amphid dendrite tips until the 2-fold stage (Schouteden et al., 2015), about an hour after the skin-driven anterior extension is complete.
evidence: The claim is based on localization data from cited prior work by Schouteden et al., 2015.

claim: During anterior extension, the dendrite tips are attached to a specific skin cell called hyp5.
source: Consistent with the notion that the dendrite tips are attached to different substrates via different molecular mechanisms, we note that during anterior extension, the tips are attached to a specific skin cell called hyp5.
evidence: The claim is based on imaging observations showing dendrite tips at the leading edge of hyp5.

claim: In the adult, the dendrite tips are embedded between different skin cells, namely hyp2 and hyp3.
source: However, in the adult, the dendrite tips are embedded between different skin cells, namely hyp2 and hyp3.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical knowledge of the adult amphid structure.

claim: hyp2/3 are born near the sensory depression and are not part of the anterior skin migration.
source: hyp2/3 are born near the sensory depression and are not part of the anterior skin migration (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations.

claim: The extension of the amphid dendrites involves a surprising level of complexity in terms of cellular and molecular mechanisms.
source: Thus, the extension of the amphid dendrites involves a surprising level of complexity in term of cellular and molecular mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from all the experimental observations presented.

claim: Surrounding tissues play profound roles in neuronal development.
source: Surrounding tissues play profound roles in neuronal development (Chao et al., 2009), and recent work has highlighted intriguing roles for the skin in shaping dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Chao et al., 2009.

claim: In Drosophila, signals from the skin shape Class IV da neurons.
source: In Drosophila, signals from the skin shape Class IV da neurons (Jiang et al., 2014; Meltzer et al., 2016; Parrish et al., 2007), and skin acts to clear debris from degenerating neurons in zebrafish (Rasmussen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Jiang et al., 2014; Meltzer et al., 2016; Parrish et al., 2007.

claim: Skin acts to clear debris from degenerating neurons in zebrafish.
source: In Drosophila, signals from the skin shape Class IV da neurons (Jiang et al., 2014; Meltzer et al., 2016; Parrish et al., 2007), and skin acts to clear debris from degenerating neurons in zebrafish (Rasmussen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Rasmussen et al., 2015.

claim: In C. elegans, the epidermis plays a role in controlling synapse density.
source: In C. elegans, the epidermis plays a role in controlling synapse density (Cherra and Jin, 2016) and positioning (Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Cherra and Jin, 2016.

claim: In C. elegans, the epidermis plays a role in controlling synapse positioning.
source: In C. elegans, the epidermis plays a role in controlling synapse density (Cherra and Jin, 2016) and positioning (Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Shao et al., 2013.

claim: The epidermis plays a critical role in patterning the elaborate dendritic arbor of the PVD neuron.
source: Furthermore, the epidermis plays a critical role in patterning the elaborate dendritic arbor of the PVD neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from prior work on PVD dendrite development.

claim: SAX-7/L1CAM functions together with MNR-1 in the epidermis to instruct the dendritic pattern of PVD.
source: Interestingly, SAX-7/L1CAM functions in this interaction. Specifically, it functions together with MNR-1 in the epidermis to instruct the dendritic pattern of PVD (Dong et al., 2013; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Dong et al., 2013 and Salzberg et al., 2013.

claim: SAX-7 is required for proper bundling of the amphid neurons.
source: SAX-7 is also required for proper bundling of the amphid neurons (Sasakura et al., 2005; Yip and Heiman, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Sasakura et al., 2005 and Yip and Heiman, 2018.

claim: The interaction between the amphid dendrites and the epidermis appears to be a simple physical attachment at a focal point defined by the rosette.
source: In our study, it remains unclear whether SAX-7 acts in the neurons, skin, or both, but the interaction between the amphid dendrites and the epidermis appears to be a simple physical attachment at a focal point defined by the rosette.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of rosette-epidermis coupling.

claim: Skin not only provides chemical signals to developing neurons, but can also provide mechanical cues that shape dendrites by physically coupling neurons to epidermal morphogenesis.
source: This example therefore suggests that skin not only provides chemical signals to developing neurons, but can also provide mechanical cues that shape dendrites by physically coupling neurons to epidermal morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing mechanical coupling between dendrites and migrating epidermis.

claim: Key structural features of the mature amphid are already seeded in the rosette before dramatic organ morphogenesis starts.
source: An interesting observation regarding the amphid rosette is that key structural features of the mature amphid are already seeded in the rosette before dramatic organ morphogenesis starts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of rosette organization and its relationship to mature amphid structure.

claim: Topological features of an organ can be specified early via short range interactions when players are local, before these features are extended over space through development.
source: Thus, topological features of an organ can be specified early via short range interactions when players are local, before these features are extended over space through development.
evidence: The claim is a general principle inferred from the observations of amphid rosette organization.

claim: In cultured hippocampal neurons, the PAR-6/PAR-3/aPKC complex is enriched at the tip of the future axon.
source: In cultured hippocampal neurons, the PAR-6/PAR-3/aPKC complex is enriched at the tip of the future axon.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from vertebrate neuron polarity studies.

claim: The PAR-6/PAR-3/aPKC complex is thought to provide local regulation of the actin cytoskeleton in vertebrate neurons.
source: The complex is thought to provide local regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (Insolera et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Insolera et al., 2011.

claim: A genetic screen in C. elegans for mutants that disrupt axon-dendrite polarity in the amphid identified unc-33, which encodes a microtubule binding protein called CRMP.
source: A genetic screen in C. elegans for mutants that disrupt axon-dendrite polarity in the amphid identified unc-33, which encodes a microtubule binding protein called CRMP (Maniar et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Maniar et al., 2011.

claim: UNC-33/CRMP localizes to the initial segment of the axon and has global effects on microtubule organization in a neuron.
source: UNC-33/CRMP localizes to the initial segment of the axon and has global effects on microtubule organization in a neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from prior work on UNC-33/CRMP.

claim: In Drosophila sensory and motor neurons, PAR-6/PAR-3/aPKC localizes to dendrites.
source: Intriguingly, in Drosophila sensory and motor neurons, PAR-6/PAR-3/aPKC localizes to dendrites (Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2005.

claim: The amphids are a bilaterally symmetric pair of sensory organs in C. elegans.
source: The amphids are a bilaterally symmetric pair of sensory organs in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of C. elegans.

claim: Each amphid consists of 12 sensory neurons and two glia cells, namely the sheath and the socket cells.
source: Each amphid consists of 12 sensory neurons and two glia cells, namely the sheath and the socket cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of C. elegans amphid structure.

claim: The 12 dendrites in an amphid form a sensory nerve, which extends from the neck to the nose tip.
source: The 12 dendrites in an amphid form a sensory nerve, which extends from the neck of the worm where the cell bodies are situated to the nose tip where most of the ciliated endings of the dendrites are exposed to the environment.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of C. elegans amphid structure.

claim: The amphid dendrites are arranged in a stereotyped order within the bundle.
source: This structure is highly organized, with the dendrites arranged in a stereotyped order within the bundle (Yip and Heiman, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Yip and Heiman, 2018.

claim: During development, amphid dendrites grow by retrograde extension, in which the dendritic tips are anchored in place at the embryonic nose while the cell bodies move posteriorly.
source: During development, these dendrites grow by retrograde extension, in which the dendritic tips are anchored in place at the embryonic nose while the cell bodies move posteriorly, extending the dendrite behind them (Heiman and Shaham, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Heiman and Shaham, 2009.

claim: The anchoring of amphid dendrite tips requires DYF-7 and DEX-1, which likely assemble a matrix in the extracellular environment.
source: The anchoring requires DYF-7 and DEX-1, which likely assemble a matrix in the extracellular environment (Heiman and Shaham, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Heiman and Shaham, 2009.

claim: In the pioneer-follower model, the pioneer neuron extends its growth cone first to explore the environment and interact with chemotropic signals and environmental guideposts.
source: In this model, the pioneer neuron extends its growth cone first to explore the environment and interact with chemotropic signals and environmental guideposts in order to establish a path to its target.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the pioneer-follower model in neurodevelopment.

claim: In the pioneer-follower model, follower neurons respond to cues from the pioneer.
source: The follower neurons respond to cues from the pioneer (Tamariz and Varela-Echavarría, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by Tamariz and Varela-Echavarría, 2015.

claim: Multiple mechanisms coordinate the interaction between the pioneer and the followers, such as selective fasciculation or juxtaparacrine signals.
source: Multiple mechanisms coordinate the interaction between the pioneer and the followers, such as selective fasciculation (Hayashi et al., 2014; Hutter, 2003; Lin et al., 1994), or juxtaparacrine signals (Jaworski and Tessier-Lavigne, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on pioneer-follower mechanisms.

claim: Coordination of neurite morphogenesis with surrounding tissues is crucial to the establishment of neural circuits.
source: Coordination of neurite morphogenesis with surrounding tissues is crucial to the establishment of neural circuits, but the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge in the field of neurodevelopment.

claim: The underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms of neurite-tissue coordination remain poorly understood.
source: Coordination of neurite morphogenesis with surrounding tissues is crucial to the establishment of neural circuits, but the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The vertex of the amphid rosette becomes the dendrite tips.
source: The vertex of the rosette, which becomes the dendrite tips, is attached to the anteriorly migrating epidermis and carried to the sensory depression, extruding the dendrites away from the neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging observations showing the rosette vertex developing into dendrite tips.

claim: The rosette vertex is attached to the anteriorly migrating epidermis and carried to the sensory depression.
source: The vertex of the rosette, which becomes the dendrite tips, is attached to the anteriorly migrating epidermis and carried to the sensory depression, extruding the dendrites away from the neuronal cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging observations and elt-1(RNAi) experiments.

claim: Multiple adhesion molecules including DYF-7, SAX-7, HMR-1 and DLG-1 function redundantly in rosette-to-epidermis attachment.
source: Multiple adhesion molecules including DYF-7, SAX-7, HMR-1 and DLG-1 function redundantly in rosette-to-epidermis attachment.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments showing redundant function of these molecules.

claim: PAR-6 promotes DYF-7 localization.
source: PAR-6 is localized to the rosette vertex and dendrite tips, and promotes DYF-7 localization and dendrite extension.
evidence: The claim is based on observations that DYF-7 localization is altered in par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: PAR-6 promotes dendrite extension.
source: PAR-6 is localized to the rosette vertex and dendrite tips, and promotes DYF-7 localization and dendrite extension.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of dendrite extension defects in par-6(M/Z) embryos.

claim: The study reveals a collective mechanism of neurite extension that is distinct from the classical pioneer-follower model.
source: Our results suggest a collective mechanism of neurite extension that is distinct from the classical pioneer-follower model and highlight the role of mechanical cues from surrounding tissues in shaping neurites.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings showing rosette-mediated collective extension.

claim: The study highlights the role of mechanical cues from surrounding tissues in shaping neurites.
source: Our results suggest a collective mechanism of neurite extension that is distinct from the classical pioneer-follower model and highlight the role of mechanical cues from surrounding tissues in shaping neurites.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings showing epidermis-driven dendrite extension.

claim: Abolishing epidermis migration by RNAi of elt-1 abolishes the extension of the amphid dendrites without affecting rosette formation.
source: Abolishing epidermis migration by RNAi of elt-1, a key transcription factor required for epidermal fate, abolishes the extension of the amphid dendrites without affecting rosette formation.
evidence: The claim is based on elt-1(RNAi) experimental results showing rosette formation but no dendrite extension.

claim: DYF-7 is made as a membrane protein but its extracellular (and functional) domain is cleaved off.
source: DYF-7 is made as a membrane protein but its extracellular (and functional) domain is cleaved off (Heiman and Shaham, 2009; Low et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by Heiman and Shaham, 2009 and Low et al., 2019.

claim: The GFP tag in the DYF-7 construct labels the extracellular domain.
source: Our GFP labels the extracellular domain.
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the DYF-7::GFP construct used in the study.

claim: It is not yet known if the cleavage of DYF-7 occurs before or after DYF-7 localizes to the dendrite tips.
source: It is not yet known if the cleavage occurs before or after DYF-7 localizes to the dendrite tips.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current knowledge about DYF-7 processing.
